result.summary: Pausanias continues his tour of Sparta, describing the temple of Hilaira and Phœbe, the house of the Tyndarids, and several hero-chapels and tombs. He tells of Dorieus's failed colonization of Sicily and then of the Orthian Artemis, her wooden statue and the Spartan flogging ritual.

scenes.title: Temple of Hilaira and Phœbe
scenes.summary: The temple of the Leucippides, with priestesses, a restored statue, a hanging egg and the weaving of Apollo's coat.

scenes.title: Castor and Pollux visit Phormio
scenes.summary: Two strangers ask Phormio for lodging; he refuses the daughter's chamber, and next day the girl is gone and statues of the twins are in her room.
scenes.stakes: Phormio's daughter's safety and honour are implied to be at risk; she vanishes.

scenes.title: Dorieus and Eryx
scenes.summary: Hero-chapels near the gates lead to the tale of Dorieus's failed Sicilian colony and Hercules's wrestling match with Eryx.
scenes.stakes: Dorieus's army is nearly annihilated by the people of Segeste.

scenes.title: Tombs and temple of Lycurgus
scenes.summary: Pausanias lists the temple of Lycurgus and nearby tombs and shrines.

scenes.title: Orthian Artemis and the flogging
scenes.summary: Pausanias argues the Spartan statue is the Tauric one, and describes the madness, the feud, and the flogging ritual.
scenes.stakes: The Spartans face pestilence and bloodshed unless the goddess is appeased with human blood.

alias_notes.explanation: Name used for both the priestesses and the goddesses Hilaira and Phœbe.
Spartan cult title of Artemis, also called Orthian Artemis.
Artemis as worshipped in the Tauric Chersonese, whose statue was claimed by Sparta.

notable_quotes.reason: Vivid description of the statue growing heavy if the scourgers spare any youth.

analysis.text: Local cult, relics and tombs tie Spartan identity to myth, with Pausanias weighing rival claims over who owns the sacred statue.
The flogging at the altar of Orthia is the Spartan ritual of endurance; Pausanias traces it to a substitute for human sacrifice.

fun_facts.text: Pausanias reasons critically about the statue's origin, arguing that the Athenians would have carried it onto their ships had they really possessed it.

language_notes.text: The Cyprian poems (Cypria) were a lost early Greek epic about events before the Trojan War, attributed to various authors.
"Touched up" and "put a new face on" mean repainting or restoring the statue, which Pausanias treats as a dubious modern practice.
Leda, wife of Tyndareus, was said to have laid an egg after Jove (Zeus) visited her as a swan; Helen and the twins were born from it.
Assa-fœtida is a strong-smelling plant resin; its odor is presumably a sign of a divine visit.
Chilo was a Spartan ephor of the sixth century BC, counted among the traditional Seven Wise Men of Greece.
Geryon's oxen were taken by Hercules as one of his labours; Scylla is the promontory on the Italian side of the Sicilian strait.
Lathria and Anaxandra's husband Aristodemus was a Heraclid; the Spartan royal houses descended from Hercules, hence the genealogy tracing Thersander back to him.
Artemisium and Salamis were naval battles of 480 BC against the Persians, here called Medes, as Greek writers often did.
Orestes and Iphigenia took the statue from the Tauric Chersonese (the Crimea) in the myth where she was priestess of a barbarian Artemis.
Brauron in Attica had a famous sanctuary of Artemis, which claimed Iphigenia left the statue there; Pausanias argues against this.
"Drawn by lot" refers to the earlier practice of choosing a human victim by lottery, replaced by ritual flogging.
Orthia means "upright"; the explanation given is that willow twigs held the statue erect.

context_notes.text: The Leucippides, Hilaira and Phœbe, were daughters of Leucippus, abducted by Castor and Pollux; here the goddesses share the name with their priestesses.
Amyclæ was a nearby Spartan town with a famous sanctuary of Apollo, for which a new tunic was woven yearly.
Castor and Pollux, sons of Tyndareus, were divine twins who often appeared to mortals disguised as strangers to test hospitality.
Dorieus, a Spartan prince and half-brother of Leonidas, left Sparta to found a colony in the west after failing to gain the throne.
Segeste (Egesta) was a Sicilian city that fought Dorieus's colonists around 510 BC.
Lycurgus was the semi-legendary Spartan lawgiver; honoring him with a temple as a god shows his status in Sparta.
Seleucus was a successor of Alexander who founded Laodicea in Syria; Pausanias traces a rival claimant statue there.
The flogging of Spartan youths at Artemis Orthia's altar was a famous, brutal endurance rite, later also a tourist spectacle.

literary_notes.text: The reader recognizes the divine twins in disguise, while Phormio treats them as ordinary travelers.
This brief aside distances Pausanias from the story, signaling that he reports tradition without vouching for it.
The balanced clauses set the divinely favored Hercules against the unaided Dorieus, whose failure is shown as lack of divine favor.
Pausanias argues his case through questions, inviting the reader to agree that the Athenian story is illogical.
The statue's growing heavy when the scourgers show mercy makes the goddess's thirst for blood tangible and enforces the rite's severity.
The statue is described as having an innate delight in human blood, giving the wooden image a will and appetite.
